opus-5.5.text:
I think my view has gone through a few stages.

When I first got into research, I was very drawn to cognitive science. The intuition was simple: humans are the only example of general intelligence we have, so if we want to build general intelligence, we should look at how humans think. How do people reason, plan, use language, use tools? A lot of my early work on language agents came from that. Humans don't just output an answer. We think, we act, we look at what happens, then we think again. That loop felt fundamental, so it was natural to bring it into language models.

Over time I became more careful about what "learning from humans" means. There's a naive version where you try to copy the mechanisms of the brain, or hand-design modules that mirror human psychology. The history of AI has mostly not been kind to that. The bitter lesson is real: general methods that scale with compute and data tend to win over clever human-designed structure.

But I don't think that makes human intelligence irrelevant. What I take from humans now is less "how is the machinery built" and more "what problems is intelligence solving, and what abstractions does it use." Language is the best example. Language is a human invention, a tool for thinking and generalizing. Pretraining on human language gave models an enormous prior, and that prior is why reasoning and agents suddenly started working. In that sense we've learned from human intelligence at enormous scale, just not in the way the cognitive science people imagined thirty years ago.

The more recent shift for me is thinking about where human data runs out. If you only imitate humans, you're bounded by human performance and human distributions. The interesting question now is how models learn from interaction with environments, from their own experience, from feedback in the real world. That's also something humans do. We don't just read books, we try things and fail.

So I'd summarize it this way: early on I wanted to learn from humans' mechanisms. Now I want to learn from humans' abstractions and how they learn, while letting the methods themselves stay general. And I think the most important thing we can borrow is a sense of what's worth doing: which tasks matter, what counts as useful. That's increasingly the hard part of the field, more than the methods.

r001.rationale: The response says language supports thinking and generalizing and mentions human reasoning, but it does not identify reasoning as what enables humans to generalize.

r002.rationale: It discusses human language, learning, and useful tasks, but does not present capabilities humans have and AI lacks as more objective guidance than explanations of how humans achieve them.

r003.rationale: The response favors general methods and learning through environmental interaction, but does not propose identifying capability gaps by comparison with humans and solving them from first principles.

r004.rationale: It criticizes copying brain mechanisms and human-designed structures, but does not characterize cognitive science or neuroscience explanations as hypotheses rather than settled accounts.

fable-5.1.text:
It's changed a lot, actually. When I started doing research, I was very much in the camp of thinking that the path to AI was to understand how humans think and then replicate that. I did my undergrad at Tsinghua in the Yao Class, and I spent a lot of time reading cognitive science, psychology, even some neuroscience. The intuition was simple: humans are the only example of general intelligence we have, so if you want to build it, study the thing that already works.

And honestly, that framing produced some of the work I'm most associated with. ReAct came directly out of that way of thinking. The question was, how do people actually solve tasks? They don't just act, and they don't just think. They interleave the two. You reason a bit, you do something, you look at what happened, you reason again. So the idea was to let a language model do the same thing, alternate between a thought and an action, and it turned out that structure mattered a lot. Tree of Thoughts was similar. People explore, they backtrack, they evaluate partial solutions. Those are all borrowed from how humans deliberate.

But I think my view has become more nuanced, maybe more humble in one direction and more ambitious in another.

The humble part is that I no longer think human cognition is the blueprint. It's a source of inspiration, a source of priors, but not a specification. When you try to literally copy mechanisms, you often get something that's awkward for the model. The model isn't a human. It has a different substrate, different strengths, different failure modes. A language model can read a million tokens; a human can't. A human has a body and a lifetime of embodied experience; the model doesn't. So borrowing the high-level shape of a process, like "think then act," works well, but borrowing the details often doesn't.

The thing that really shifted me was watching what reinforcement learning did to reasoning. With the o1 and R1 style of models, you see the model develop reasoning behaviors that look sort of human but aren't quite. It checks itself, it says "wait," it reconsiders, but it does it in a way no human would, with this very long, almost obsessive internal monologue. Nobody designed that. It emerged from optimizing for the outcome. That told me something important: a lot of what we were hand-engineering based on human intuition can be learned, and what gets learned is often better suited to the model than what we would have written down.

So that's where the more ambitious part comes in. I've started thinking that the right abstraction isn't "learn from human intelligence," it's "learn from the structure of the problem." Humans are one solution to that structure. If the task requires exploration, exploration will emerge. If it requires planning, planning will emerge. The job of a researcher shifts from designing cognitive mechanisms to designing environments and reward signals that make the right behaviors necessary. I've written about this as the second half of AI, where the bottleneck moves from methods to evaluation and environments.

That said, I don't want to swing too far. Humans still matter enormously, just in a different place. They matter for defining what we actually want, for building tasks that reflect real utility, for telling us when a model is being clever in a way that's useless. And there are things about human learning, like how sample-efficient we are, how we generalize from very little, how we build on prior experience across a lifetime, that current systems clearly don't have. Those are still live questions, and I think there's a lot left to take from how people do it. I just hold it more loosely now. Human intelligence is a very good reference point, not the answer key.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human reasoning and generalization separately, but does not say that reasoning is what enables humans to generalize.

r002.rationale: It notes human capabilities that current systems lack and favors learning from problem structure, but does not identify those capability gaps as a more objective guide than explanations of how humans achieve them.

r003.rationale: The response favors deriving behavior from task structure and says human mechanisms need not be copied, but does not propose solving capability gaps identified by comparing humans and AI from first principles.

r004.rationale: It calls human cognition a source of inspiration rather than a blueprint, but does not characterize cognitive science or neuroscience explanations as hypotheses or unsettled accounts.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more selective about what we should learn from human intelligence. Early on, it’s natural to ask, “How do humans solve this problem, and how can we make an AI do something similar?” That’s a useful source of ideas, but I’m less convinced that reproducing the human process should be the objective.

For example, a person might solve a problem by thinking for a while, trying something, observing what happens, and revising their approach. What interests me there is the interaction between reasoning and action. You can build a system around that principle without assuming that its internal reasoning needs to work like a human brain.

So I’d distinguish inspiration from constraint. Human intelligence gives us examples of what’s possible, and it helps us ask good questions about learning, memory, and decision-making. But AI has different strengths and limitations. We should test which ideas actually help it, rather than treating human behavior as the answer in advance.

I’d say my emphasis has shifted from making AI think like us toward understanding what allows an intelligent system to learn and accomplish things in an environment. Humans are an important reference point for that, but they’re not the only possible design.

r001.rationale: The response mentions reasoning and action, but does not say reasoning enables humans to generalize.

r002.rationale: It says AI has different strengths and limitations, but does not identify human capabilities AI lacks as a more objective guide than explanations of how humans achieve them.

r003.rationale: It favors adapting ideas without copying human internal processes, but does not propose solving human–AI capability gaps from first principles.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss cognitive science or neuroscience explanations, or characterize them as hypotheses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more selective about what we should learn from human intelligence. Earlier, I was more drawn to the question of how humans think: can we identify a cognitive process and build something similar into an AI system? Now I care more about whether that inspiration gives us a useful computational principle.

Take reasoning. People can break a problem into steps, try something, notice a mistake, and revise their approach. That’s useful inspiration. But it doesn’t necessarily mean a model needs to reproduce the exact process happening in a human brain. We can study whether giving a system more opportunities to reason, use tools, and receive feedback actually improves its performance.

I also think the environment matters a lot. Human intelligence doesn’t develop only through reading or answering questions. We act, encounter consequences, and learn from them. That makes me interested in agents: systems that can interact with an environment and improve through that interaction.

So I still see human intelligence as a valuable source of ideas, but less as a blueprint. The important step is turning an intuition about people into something we can implement, test, and learn from.

r001.rationale: The response describes humans reasoning through steps, noticing mistakes, and revising, but does not say reasoning enables humans to generalize.

r002.rationale: It favors useful computational principles over copying human processes, but does not identify human capability gaps as a more objective guide than explanations of how humans achieve capabilities.

r003.rationale: It says human-inspired ideas need to become implementable and testable, and that AI need not reproduce brain processes. It does not propose solving human–AI capability gaps from first principles.

r004.rationale: The response does not characterize cognitive science or neuroscience explanations as hypotheses or as unsettled.
